utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, you're continuing with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. We are continuing

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Popovic. Can you hear me? Can you hear me now, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It seems we can't get the transmission across.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I can hear you too.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Popovic, yesterday we talked about the events during the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992. You said that people gathered in Crkvina. Mr. Popovic, can you please wait until I finish my question. We had great problems yesterday. I was checking the transcript, and there are quite a number of mistakes. So please, if you could just speak a bit more slowly and keep your answers brief. Try to be as accurate as possible when using the terms "we," "they," "the other side," that sort of thing. We both understand each other. We know what happened in Samac. But for the sake of the Trial Chamber and for the transcript, please try to keep it as accurate as possible and specify the Serb side, the Muslim side, the Croat side, or whatever it is you're referring to in the context. Thank you very much. Mr. Popovic, in Crkvina, in the period prior to the night between the 16th and 17th of April, did you notice any JNA units? Were there any JNA units around in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the JNA units are concerned, what I can say is that throughout that period, there were forces that were withdrawing from Croatia and Slovenia. They were crossing in groups. Soldiers were crossing, and they were staying in the area. They would refresh themselves. They would tell us stories about what happened in those areas, that barracks had been abandoned or taken, and they would return to their homes. And I can also add that the army was being evacuated from those areas, and across the bridge in Samac, the army was leaving for Sarajevo and Banja Luka. I can't say exactly how many of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. That suffices. Mr. Popovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What's the name of the JNA unit in the Samac area? Was there any particular unit stationed there? What was its name?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The 17th Tactical Group, how many detachments did it comprise?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that according to the military structure, there were supposed to be six or seven. Now, some people refer to them as detachments, some as battalions, but in that area, they were based in the general Samac and Pelagicevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the area of your own local commune, Crkvina, which detachment was there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crkvina Battalion. The Crkvina Battalion was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us not confuse these names. Is there any particular detachment name associated with it, the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd detachment? Which one was in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 5th detachment. I'm not a hundred per cent certain, but that's how I referred to it, the Crkvina Detachment. It was perhaps the 1st or the 2nd or the 5th. I can't answer this accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of that detachment in Crkvina was?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main commander [as interpreted] was Marko Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do you mean the main commander? In which period?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think until May, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Take it easy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a matter of accuracy of transcript. The witness said "the first commander was," not "the main commander." Because after that, he was replaced with another person. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, please speak slowly. When you say the month of May, it can be both 1992 and 1993. Until which May specifically was he the commander of the 2nd Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the month of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, were any soldiers present in Crkvina? How can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As there had been mobilisation prior to that, through the secretariat for National Defence, the units were filled up. I was talking about Croats and Muslims wanting or not wanting to join the units. There were loyal people too, and a number of those people was in Crkvina too. Crkvina, as a local commune, was mobilised with a number of members who had been members of the Territorial Defence, in terms of their assignment. I can't define this precisely, but there were people from Crkvina there, from Pisar. They had their own command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please try to speak a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. The role of the local commune --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, can you hold on, please. My question was brief and very clear. Let us not waste time, please. Prior to the 16th of April, did you see that any soldiers, legitimate soldiers, or organs of the JNA, the 1st or 2nd Detachment, were present in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see. We, at the local commune, as the local commune, it had the task and the role in case of war to protect the civilian population, in case of shelling. Innocent people, women and children, were to be protected. Food was to be provided, as well as the protection for those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You described yesterday how the conflict started in the night of the 17th of April, 1992. Can you please tell me: What sort of units did you see in Crkvina? What military units? Can you describe that? And specifically, I want to know if there were any tanks in Crkvina at that time.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no tanks at that time in Crkvina. Checkpoints had been set up in Crkvina at the crossroads towards Gradacac. Uniformed police officers appeared there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which checkpoints? Which barricades? And who had organised those?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station in Samac were the ones who had set them up. And then there were locals present there surprised by what was going on. They were standing about. And in that period of time, they were performing checks as to who was leaving Samac and who was entering Samac, or that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for the specific period, we are talking about the period of time after the 17th of April, 1992, to all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You told me that the next day, on the 18th, you went to the Pik factory. Who called you to go there and who took you there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to -- but I couldn't manage. I, with Mr. Bogdanovic, who was simply the alpha and omega of the mobilisation in Samac, he was a friend, and he would come to Crkvina. And he called me and we went to his car and we drove to the Pik factory. I found a number of people there, as I described. There were people gathering there in that area. Why there specifically? Why at the Pik? Because it was in the outskirts. And it was safer in some way than the town itself, so that's where I came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who exactly did you find there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. Just for the sake of clarity: On page 6, line 1, could Mr. Popovic be specific when -- maybe it's just the translation, but it says that: Mr. Bogdanovic, who was simply the alpha and omega of the mobilisation in Samac. We all know Latin, but I think for the sake of clarity, could we have an understanding what Mr. Popovic means when he says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, did you hear the Honourable Judge Williams and her question? Can you please explain?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Milos Bogdanovic was the chief or the head of the secretariat for National Defence or the secretariat for National Defence, and he was linked with the military component, as they refer to it, so it was under his leadership, from his stories, when the 17th Tactical Group was present there, he was the person who was in communication and who was communicating with the gentleman from that specific Tactical Group. He had all the plans, which means that everything was done according to his directives or according to the plans that the secretariat for National Defence had. So practically, he was in charge. That's why I said that he was the alpha and omega, and no one else could interfere with mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. As you've told us, he called you and you went to the Pik factory. Can you please tell me: Which persons exactly did you find there? Can you give us the names? How many people were there? What sort of people were they? What were their backgrounds? What were their jobs? Can you please tell us about the first few hours of the 18th of April there. Please tell us whatever you know about it, what you talked about and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there with Mr. Bogdanovic, we parked our car near the barn and we ran over to the main building of the Pik because there was shooting and bullets were flying all around. The building had one floor, and on the first floor I found Mr. Mirko Jovanovic. Blagoje Simic was there too, Simeon Simic. There were other people there, other gentlemen who were there from the surrounding villages. People simply came there to see what was going on, because that was one of the roads practically into the city, the town. There was chaos. People were coming in and going out. So everyone was talking about what it was that was happening, and in what way fighting could break out in the town itself. I know that people were talking about how to secure the infrastructure, how things could be kept to function in terms of food, bread, and health protection, in order to keep the town and its surroundings going and functioning normally, so there wouldn't be any breakdown in the normal functions of life, so that life could go on. Everyone agreed that this was important and that the whole thing had to be stopped as quickly as possible, so there would be no bloodshed. So as to stop the undesirable consequences from ensuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, was a body set up on that occasion? The whole group, did you spontaneously continue working or did you sort of begin to organise yourselves? Can you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. The body probably was transformed into terms of its name into a Crisis Staff, but as far as the people who were present there, and I must point out Mr. Mirko Jovanovic, who was the then president of the Executive Board and of the newly created -- I mean the municipality of Serbian Samac, he was in charge and he was the head of government. He said that a body should be set up, whether it was -- whether it would be called a staff, a civilian organ, one organ which could secure the functioning of the economy, all I've talked about now, the functioning of the educational institutions, of the health institutions. And he said we should see which people exactly were there at that moment who could make sure that the whole thing kept functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, so was a Crisis Staff set up at that point?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me whether I, as a man who was always around or near them, whether I would accept to be with them, to join them in that team. I said I had nothing against it, if I can place myself at your disposal, gentlemen. I have worked before in the economy, and I was active in the political life too. At that moment, Blagoje Mirko Jovanovic and Savo Popovic, at first, the three of us, we sat down and we started thinking in what way specifically we could keep things functioning and which people exactly we could involve in our work over the next period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So who were the people that you had involved?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the economy, Stevan Todorovic, Perica Krstanovic, the distribution; and as far as the health institutions were concerned, we engaged a number of doctors; as far as education, Simeon Simic and Lazar from Donji Zabar; Mirkic for the economy, because he was associated with the economy; from Pelagicevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, can you please slow down. We had some technical problems here. Let us start from the beginning. Tell me first: You said that Stevan Todorovic was in charge of economic affairs. Tell me first -- please wait. Let me finish, please. Let's start from the beginning. Do you know whether Stevan Todorovic was appointed head of the public security station in Samac? Wait, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, please slow down. Do you know whether the Serbian MUP was established in March of 1992 at the level of the Republic of Srpska at the time? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were the civilian authorities in Samac - and by this, I refer to the Crisis Staff or any other structures of the Serbian municipality - in charge of commanding the police?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether Stevan Todorovic, at the time that you describe of things taking place at Pik, was he involved as a member of the Crisis Staff in the later work of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't see Stevan Todorovic. He appeared later, for a brief period of time, and he used to go and we couldn't possibly establish any communication with him or talk to him about what was happening and how he was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to what you said before. Since the transcript says that you stated that Stevan Todorovic was appointed for economic affairs on this Crisis Staff, was that true? Can you please explain that slowly. Which people were appointed to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were: Blagoje Simic; Savo Popovic; Mirko Jovanovic, as president of the Executive Board from the previous composition; and also, in this new body, Stevan Todorovic was appointed chief the public security station. Therefore, he could not be appointed to be in charge of economic affairs. Rather, I said that it was Lazar Mikic, from Donji Zabar, I don't know exactly, was in charge of economic affairs, and another person was mentioned, that it would be advisable to have him on board. And then later we agreed that a man who was at the head of the civilian protection should also be on the Crisis Staff. Later it turned out that that was Miro Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Simeon Simic a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simeon Simic joined later. He wasn't there immediately, but the four that I mentioned were there on the spot, and we proposed other people, even Fadil of another ethnicity was proposed to become a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which Fadil?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brother-in-law of Simo Zaric. His name was Topcagic, I think. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Topcagic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His last name was Topcagic. So this body, only after they left to Uniglas a few days later, given the circumstances prevailing at the time, was fully established and was supposed to start operating. However, this Crisis Staff was never able to become functional with all its members, and I know that Mr. Simo Zaric came a few days later, and he was simply supposed -- and he was in a certain way promoted as chief for national security in the area of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Popovic: Since you mentioned Perica Krstanovic from the power utility company and other professionals, how would you describe the operation of the Crisis Staff, both in the narrow and the broader terms? Who were those people? Who had the voting right? And could quite simply in those first weeks of war conflict, how did you function, and what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: We first had to see which people -- on which people we can count and what companies were of vital importance that were to function in this initial period in order to provide an unhindered supply for citizens. That means schools, health care, staples, commodities. So we agreed that all these major companies that in fact remained without their management, that we appoint coordinators to these companies, and we decided that Perica Krstanovic would take charge of power utility company, Dr. Nogic for health care. So I wouldn't enumerate all of them. In a nutshell, all companies had their coordinators. For example, the trade also had its coordinator taking charge of providing supplies for the population. Therefore, we asked these people to come. We discussed this with them and explained to them what their tasks in the forthcoming period were to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Popovic: For how long did the Crisis Staff function in that -- on that location, and did it move to another location later?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We remained about two or three days - I cannot say exactly - but since the space that we used was not safe, we decided to move to Uniglas, which is about 100 metres downwards across the railway track, and this facility had a shelter. And we were in a sort of way isolated from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have a lawyer on your Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there was a suggestion while we were still in Pik and I think Mr. Mirko Jovanovic said that, and proposed Mr. Mitar Mitrovic from Obudovac, who was a lawyer with the agricultural cooperative. He was an ambitious man, with good prospects, and at the time we believed that it would be advisable to have such a person for legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did Bozo Ninkovic do?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozo Ninkovic was entrusted with taking care of technical matters relating to information, so he was supposed to be at hand to us if we needed something, since at the time he worked for the Ministry of Defence, or rather, the secretariat for defence, and he spent the whole time with us and he provided his services to all of us there at the Pik and in the Uniglas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the first period, did the Crisis Staff take the decision to impose a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not adopt any decisions. We simply discussed what is to be -- what was to be done in terms of organisation. But as for any decision on introducing, we didn't take such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Popovic: What did the Crisis Staff do regarding the Serbian detainees in Odzak in April and May? Who did it appeal to?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this problem of people detained in the area of Odzak municipality was kind of imposed on us, because there was -- communications were totally cut off across the river Bosna with the Serbian population in Trnjak, Dubica, Novi Grad, and other places, Serb-populated places. They -- the detainees, about 4.000 of Serbs, were located in one place, and our task was to use the media and inform --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Popovic. You are speaking much too fast, and we cannot have everything you say on the transcript. I know that you have to tell us a lot, but please be calm and explain this slowly. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I mentioned that according to some information, there were about 4.000 Serbian detainees in Novi Grad. So let's say that was a camp. And our role and task were to inform the general public, through the media, and to request that these people be released and to cross over to the territory of Samac. And in doing that, we asked television, the press. I know that a man from the Oslobodjenje newspaper called me, who used to live in Samac. His name was Mato. He asked me what was going on in Novi Grad and what was going on in Samac. I gave him information and asked him to write articles in his newspapers demanding that these people be released and be let go wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, I presume that you also appealed both to the international and domestic public concerning the situation with the Serbs in Odzak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Whomever we knew, and whenever we could get in touch with international organisations, we sent faxes demanding them to intervene for those people to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you also addressed the federal organs in Yugoslavia concerning our people in Odzak. Just say yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Popovic: On the Crisis Staff, did you extensively discuss these issues concerning the Serbs in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were preoccupied with that issue that we spent most of the time dealing with, trying to find a way how to bring these people back, because their families or relatives managed to pull out before that or remained on this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you get in touch with the representatives of the Croatian side regarding the release of people in Odzak; and if you did, who initiated these contacts?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew, I believe - I don't believe I know - that that was taken care of by Mr. Tadic and Simo Zaric. They maintained contacts through communication channels in order to find a way to pull these people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know anything about the behaviour of Stevan Todorovic and his police and the volunteers from Serbia in these first few weeks in Samac? Specifically, were there any arrests?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Stevan Todorovic, as a civilian authority, did not accept, and Stevan and his police acted independently, surely they had - and that turned out to be true later - they made some arrests when they -- when the police station and other municipal institutions were captured, lists were found, and they knew which people from the SDA and HDZ were linked and whether they should be arrested in order to acquire information who else was involved in the SDA and HDZ, HVO formations, as they were used to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Popovic: What do you know about a tragic event in Crkvina sometime around the 8th of May, 1992, between the 7th and 8th of May, 1992, when a number of non-Serbian persons were killed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About this horrendous event that we all comment on, I heard only a few days later, because that was kept secret by Stevan Todorovic's police, and those other men who were involved in that, and we found out who committed this horrible crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. We had an interruption. The last thing that we heard from you is that you learnt who was the perpetrator of that terrible crime. Please continue, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later, we learnt who the perpetrator of that crime was. We didn't know immediately who was involved in all that. We only found out about that a few days later, and we demanded that it be established precisely, that it be condemned, and the perpetrators to be brought to justice. I know that Mr. Savo Cancarevic, a police commander, was involved, probably somebody from the military was also involved in a way in this horrendous murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He's using a lot of phrases: We, "we demanded that it be established precisely," whatever that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "We didn't know who was involved." And then "I know that Savo Cancarevic, a police commander, was involved, probably someone from the military was also involved in this horrendous murder." Is he saying that they -- Savo Cancarevic was shooting people to or ... Nothing is clear in this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Can you ask the witness to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you are a serious man. You discharged various functions in your lifetime. Please, this is absolutely chaotic what we have on the transcript. Can you speak at this pace that I am talking to you now. Please answer this question, but slowly. When you say "we," who are you referring to? To the Crisis Staff? And the people from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please wait a minute. Let us clarify what you said. We have a confusion here about what you said, Mr. Popovic. Did we understand you correctly that Savo Cancarevic, the police commander, and some other bodies from the military, were in charge of investigating the crime? Is that what you said? Wait a minute, please. Who, according to your knowledge, since you said that there were rumours about that, who committed this crime, as far as you know, that all the civilian authorities and all the residents of Samac condemned? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I learnt, and the Crisis Staff learned about that a few days later, that that was committed by Lugar, a man called Lugar. And what I was just telling you about the investigation --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, let us go back to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was investigating this crime?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This crime was investigated by the police commander, Savo Cancarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who had committed the crime in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar was the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In those days when the crime was committed, did you enter the hall or the premises where the crime occurred, personally?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't enter. I was at the Uniglas building, and I was in no position to be where the crime took place. So I was not in Crkvina. I was in Samac, at the Uniglas building. And I said that I had learnt, like all the others, several days later after the vicious crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have a brother?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Ranko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was he a police officer in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ranko was an active-duty policeman. He was an officer with the police at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I asked you all these questions because there is a Prosecution witness who got the names all muddled up. So this is an opportunity for us to clarify this once and for all. That's why I asked you this question.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, the police authorities, what did they do upon learning of the murder in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I said and mentioned the name of Mr. Savo Cancarevic. He was engaged in some way. Now, who he had received orders from, I don't know, to carry out the entire investigation. He didn't tell the public about what had happened and who had been hurt and who had been behind the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, on or about the 19th of May, the JNA left the area; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which units -- which unit was set up as part of the army of Republika Srpska in the Samac area at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Posavina Brigade was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was its first commander, the first commander of the Posavina Brigade? I suppose we're talking about the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We named it the 1st, but later it was renamed as the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Because Brcko also had a brigade, and that brigade was referred to as the 1st, and the 2nd was the Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was the first commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While the Tactical Group was present, it was in some way Mr. Stevan Nikolic was the coordinator of all those activities concerning --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Please, listen carefully to my question. The JNA left. Stevan Nikolic left. After the 19th of May, 1992, that's my question, according to your information, who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjevic. Is Colonel Djurdjevic a relation of yours?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That leads me to assume that you -- the two of you are close and that you discussed certain details.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How long was Colonel Djurdjevic the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only for a brief period of time, because he was exposed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Go easy. You'll explain everything.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was under pressure from Mr. Todorovic, Crni, Debeli, and the others. They said that he was inept because he was a communications officer by profession, and they said that he couldn't be in charge of a tactical -- I mean a brigade like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You said he was an engineer by profession, is that correct, not a communications officer?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the role of the Superior Command and Colonel Dencic concerning the appointment of Djurdjevic first to the 2nd Posavina Brigade and then later to a different position? He was your relation, so probably you did discuss that at the time. Tell us what you know about it. Was there a Superior Command?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of military structure, we all belonged to the East Bosnia Corps, and Colonel Dencic was the chief of that corps, the commander. Everything that concerned the brigades, down the chain of command, orders were coming from the corps. Mr. Djurdjevic had been appointed by Mr. Dencic, who was the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Colonel Djurdjevic, which position was he appointed to after leaving Samac, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the unfortunate events that had occurred and his forced dismissal by the group I talked about, who came in with a number of their own battalion commanders and demanded that he leave his duty, that he resign immediately and leave his position. Later I found out from him that he had been transferred or, rather, assigned to the 1st Bosnian [as interpreted] in Brcko. He was appointed the brigade commander there. That brigade was bigger and stronger than the one in Samac, in terms of its structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript. Page 20, line 22. Instead of 1st Bosnian in Brcko, it should be 1st Posavina Brigade in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 1st Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were at the Crisis Staff at the heating plant when Colonel Djurdjevic came to see you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who else was there with you? And can you describe what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there. Blagoje was there too. I was there, Mitar Mitrovic was there, Simeon was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Slowly, please. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozo Ninkovic is the man who was in charge of intelligence and information. Mr. Djurdjevic came in. He greeted us. He told us about problems related to supplies. The army didn't have enough food or equipment. They were running out of uniforms. All those problems related to that. He told us about them. We looked through the window and we saw vehicles arriving. They pulled over, and Stevan Todorovic came out, escorted by several battalion commanders. They came upstairs. They sat down. The commanders were standing there, armed. He said that Commander Djurdjevic could no longer remain in his position as the head of the Posavina Brigade, because there was another person who was better suited or more qualified to run the thing, and that was Crni. He said the whole thing had been arranged at corps level. Mr. Djurdjevic, Mico, told me: Please don't get involved. Let the thing run its course. Mr. Todorovic said: Unless we have this our way, the way we have requested, and the way battalion commanders want it to be, there could be great problems. He said that we, as a civilian organ, were not to interfere with the military component or the military structures. After that, those gentlemen left. Crni took over, according to our information, took over the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, and Mr. Dencic, as a superior commander at corps level, gave him the rank of lieutenant colonel, because he had no rank, so he was not qualified to command the army. Now, how that had been agreed or who had been behind it, those were the orders that reached the Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to your information, Stevan Todorovic, did he have any relation to the military structures in Belgrade? If you know what sort of relationship there was, tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, whenever he came to see us, he would phone certain persons and he would say: I know this general or that general, General Bajic, Colonel Jeremic, people like those. He did drop a couple of other names. Whether he was directly linked with them or not, we don't know, but he threatened us all the time that if we tried anything to interfere with the military structures or the police, we would be stopped. He stalled our work and he forbade us to interfere with the police and military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, how would you describe the relationship between you, personally, and your colleagues from the Crisis Staff with Stevan Todorovic and the volunteers? We're speaking about the period of May and June. How would you describe the relationship? Were you on friendly terms? Were you allies?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Stevan Todorovic as a man who was abrasive. He liked to put himself first. He thought he could do anything. And I had the feeling that he had used his connections in Serbia, and those people who arrived in the Samac area, as a team that was supposed to work with him, to cooperate with him as some sort of a force that would secure a certain sense of safety for us. However, it turned out that those people who had arrived were simply there for his own purposes, and to all of us they were just a menace to our lives. No one was supposed to stand up against them or oppose them. Their lives would be in danger, or those of their families. He tried to eliminate all those who didn't share his opinions, who didn't share the opinions of Stevan Todorovic. He tried to have these people eliminated from the structures, from the civilian structures and from Samac municipality. You could feel this, and you could see this, because this had happened with the late Milos Bogdanovic, who, in a way, posed a problem for Stevan Todorovic. He was an obstacle. There were games going on in the wings, and this man had been accused, falsely accused, as it turned out later, and they arranged that he could no longer be the head of defence ministry, or rather, the secretariat for National Defence. Another thing I need to add: In my opinion, the president of the Executive Board, Mirko Jovanovic, was also removed by force, who, on one occasion, banged his fist against the table and said: I am the president of the Executive Board, not you, Mr. Todorovic. It's down to me. I'm the one calling the shots as far as the civilian structures are concerned. And I will not let you, the police, interfere. After several days, after receiving threats from Crni and his people who had arrived, Mirko Jovanovic had to step down as the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, as the corridor had been broken through towards the end of June 1992, and the Krajina Corps entered its area, the area of responsibility of Odzaci [phoen] and later also Samac, what did you and Blagoje Simic do concerning the volunteers? Who did you get in touch with, and what was the result of your contacts? Who did you talk to about this problem you had with this particular group?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I'm a man who was present at the staff, as we refer to it now, I knew what was being done and what the aims of that group were, that it was a group of plunderers and looters, renegades, practically. Now, whether he was in charge, whether he commanded them, whether he took part in their operations or just whether he was carrying out their orders, it was Stevan Todorovic. I proposed to Blagoje that we should go and see Mr. Colonel Novica Simic, who I think was a major at that point, or lieutenant colonel, in Odzak, to talk to him and ask him to make it possible for us to go and see General Talic and request assistance from the general as regarded the military structures, because we could no longer put up with what Crni was doing. So an appointment was made for us to immediate General Talic. Mr. Blagoje Simic and I went to the village of Osjecani, near Doboj, where the command was based, the headquarters. General Talic was there. We told the general about all the problems that Samac, as a municipality, was facing at the level of civilian government. We told him about what was happening in relation to the 1st [as interpreted] Posavina Brigade. We appealed for -- we appealed to him to provide assistance. He listened to our story and he told us that he knew what had been going on over there. He said he would send over Mr. Mile Beronja - I think he was a major at that point, and he was the head of the 1st Tactical Group in Odzak. After several days, because communications had already been set up with the 1st Krajina Corps, through military communications, a number of dismissals were made, and Mr. Beronja was appointed commander of our Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, please tell us: When Commander Beronja was appointed, were some other officers appointed to security tasks in the brigade at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that was, in a way, subordinated, because Crni was the commander, so it was only logical to expect that Beronja, as the new brigade commander, would appoint his own man and put his own man in charge of security issues. And he brought Mr. Jez, who was, I think, a captain, and I think he had been a security officer at the Laktas Brigade, part of the Tactical Group in Odzak, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, on page 25, line 4 of the transcript, you said the 1st Posavina Brigade. Actually, it should be the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Are we talking about the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, tell me: At that time, were the volunteers removed from the territory of Samac municipality when Beronja was appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - I'm speaking for myself - Beronja did a kind of purging of these battalions from these volunteers. But in a certain way, individuals were still present in the area of Samac, because somehow they should have been expelled and removed from the territory of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were they expelled?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, we had technical problems. Could you please go back to the beginning. I asked you: Were they expelled from the area?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were removed, and quite simply were not allowed to stay any longer in the territory of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you stop here, and then we shall proceed slowly. Do you know about the operation which resulted in the military administration in Odzak in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the liberation or, rather, when the 1st Krajina Corps entered the area of Odzak municipality, these contacts were established connected with Samac, and several days later, Colonel Vujinovic came to Samac. He was the assistant commander for civilian affairs of the 1st Krajina Corps. He requested our Crisis Staff to second a number of people to be dispatched to this area and become involved in organising civilian life there and the acceptance of people to return, the people who had left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the order by General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, to introduce military administration in July -- in June 1992? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: One correction. I was referring to July 1992. Mr. Popovic, did you go to Odzak as an economist? Did you go on of your own volition or as a tourist or on orders or within the framework of your work obligation? Can you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the colonel's request from the Samac municipality to have certain number of people transferred to this area, I was given a decision within my work obligation to go there and do certain jobs in the area of Odzak municipality. So I got this decision from our ministry. At the time, it was necessary, and Miroslav Tadic came a few days later to take care of this civilian protection domain, and Simo Zaric came as a person in charge of both civilian and military security, in order to be present in Odzak municipality. And those were our assignments made by our ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, when you say "our ministry," can you be more specific? We have people here who don't know what "our ministry" is.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the secretariat for defence of Samac municipality. That is the organ that we received --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Wait a second. Are you referring to the department of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In Odzak, that was under military administration, were representatives of other surrounding municipalities, as well as representatives from the villages in Odzak municipality, can you tell us the names of the people who were on the military administration council and what kind of duties they discharged? When you tell us the names, since we have the transcript in English, could you please pronounce their names slowly so that we can have them correctly on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Odzak. I reported to the commander of this formation, and I said that I had been given a written decision to report to him. He told me: Please have a seat. He explained to me what the role and the task of that body that I was supposed to run, as a man who came from Samac, in order to establish a body or an organ, to include representatives of local communes in the territory of Odzak municipality, and that involved Ljubo Goranovic, from Trnjak; Aco Minic, from Donja Dubica; Dusko Galic, from the town of Odzak; Miso Pavic, from Novi Grad; Rakic, from Svilaj, I don't remember his first name; Kojic, from Josava, I think his first name was Milenko.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation didn't get the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Slowly, Mr. Popovic, please. The interpreters, because you are really speaking at a deadly pace -- please name the names slowly. They didn't get the name of the village. Did you see Gnionice? Slowly, Mr. Popovic. There was a large number of people involved in this council, mainly representatives from local communes of Odzak municipality and of the surrounding municipalities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military administration was the man who approved all these appointments and who ran the whole military administration work.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object. I'd move to strike his answer. The counsel is testifying at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. That was a very leading question. Can you rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. I do apologise. I tried to control the witness, you know, because he is so confused and he's speaking with unnecessary detail. So I tried to put him in tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he asks one question at a time, it would help, instead of these long questions that have five different issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we get back to the witness so that he can give the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Popovic, tell me: You already explained that there were a lot of people on the council discharging various duties. Later we shall discuss a number of documents relating to this. Could you please explain to the Chamber how the military administration functioned. Explain what the role of the commander of the military administration was, and tell us his name, of course.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Tactical Group commander was at the head. Initially it was Major or Lieutenant Colonel Novica Simic. And as they were rotating at the head of the Tactical Group, equally, that person would also assume the role of the commander of the military administration. Mr. Simic was replaced by another commander. Myself and the other people on the council were -- had the task and the role to organise life for the people who were supposed to return and who started to return to their respective local communes. In other words, we were supposed to organise the infrastructure, which means electricity, water, regular supplies for the population, education system, health care system, civilian protection, the Red Cross, and other utility affairs within the domain or that had impact on civilian life. Everything else was exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Tactical Group command, and this Tactical Group had its own rules or, rather, orders how -- relating to the behaviour of the civilian sector, governing how and in what way we could come into or out of this zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, we had another interruption. I apologise. As members of the council, were you allowed to take any independent decisions in the domain of work that you took care of in Odzak? Can you explain that, just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not allowed to do anything independently. Whatever idea we had, we had to present this to the commander of the military administration, and it was up to him to listen to us and then approve or not approve. Whatever was to be done in this territory, we needed full endorsement from the commander of the Tactical Group, who was at the head of this administration. Everything was divided according to their areas of responsibility of various brigades in their respective zones of responsibility. They have their own rounded areas, and neither -- the civilians were not allowed to cross from one zone to another without explicit permission from security organs in the areas where their units were located. So practically, we were all under the control in terms of movement and working, of this council and of the civilians who at the time lived in the area of Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Under whose control were you, as members of the council?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were under the control of security organs of the Tactical Group 1, or if we move downwards, that was under the control of security organs of their units, in their respective areas. There was a man in charge of security in a particular area. You have to report to this person if you move onwards to another local commune, where another unit was deployed. You had to first report to another security organ --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say "the Tactical Group," you were referring to the military unit that was in charge in the area of responsibility of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please be precise in order to avoid any confusion in the transcript. Tell me, please, for how long were you personally member of the military administration council? Tell us the exact period. When did you become member of the council and for how long did you discharge this duty? Just give me the time frame, without any further explanations.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discharged this duty until the end of February or March 1993, and then changes were introduced in running this military administration, and I became just a member of the personnel in charge of a specific centre, and the council itself ceased to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you become member?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From July --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which year? July which year, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: July 1992, between the 20th and the 25th of July, 1992, until the end of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you came to Odzak, were there any residents there from the territory of Odzak? Who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, upon the arrival of these units of the 1st Krajina Corps, a number of civilians returned with them. But mainly there was no one there from the former residents that used to live there before the units entered the town. So two or three days prior to their arrival in Odzak, they all left, and they just took the belongings that they could carry with them, because the HVO was present in this area. And I heard that an order had been issued that everyone must leave and take with them a number of Serbs that they kept in detention in Odzak in Novi Grad, and that they took them with you [as interpreted], and that later they were in the area of Slavonski Brod or other parts of Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Popovic, that an order was issued, who issued the order on withdrawal of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that that was done by the HVO, in agreement with the authorities and commands from Croatia, because they operated in concert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say "Odzak," are you referring to the entire territory of Odzak municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire territory of Odzak municipality, where Croats, Muslims, and a number of Serbs used to live. And these Serbs -- the Serbs who were detained were taken away with them before the territory was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Popovic: I would like now to discuss with you a document that you have provided for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Of Defence document ODZ-1. It was already provided to our learned friends from the Prosecution. The title of document is, "The obligatory instructions on tasks of the military administration's organs, public state organs and other bodies," issued on October 10th, 1992, by the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. So very briefly I will discuss a couple of articles of this document. These are three copies for the Trial Chamber and two copies for the registry, and the Court officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, the registrar in Belgrade, who is sitting next do you, can she please show you the document? Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That means we can proceed discussing the document. Mr. Popovic, can you please tell me: When you saw this obligatory instruction for the first time, in which period of time? Tell me briefly. Which time of year?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Maybe we should have a copy put on the ELMO so the accused persons can see what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's correct. But I think -- Mr. Usher, you can put on the ELMO, please, the B/C/S version. But I'm -- I don't think that it would be possible, because we suffered the same problems yesterday. When we have a document here on the ELMO, and then when we push the button video evidence, we are receiving the videolink from Belgrade, actually, the -- actually, the witness by himself. So we cannot see this document here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can proceed, because what is important is that the witness has got a copy at the table where he's sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, Mr. Popovic. You said that towards the end of 1991 you first found out about this document. Can you please tell me, if you look at Article 1 -- I will read the first item of this document: "The organs of military administration, in cooperation with republican and state organs, carry out administration, expert, and other types of work regulated by laws and regulations based on law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the booth please be provided with a copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Popovic: What did this mean in practice? Can you please explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this meant, in practice, is that all these segments were governed by the military administration. As a council, we were an executive body that was supposed to act on these instructions and carry out our tasks in accordance with our instructions. We didn't have any written orders. We only received oral instructions. You are to do this and that. You should carry out this and that. You should organise the reception of returnees. You should cooperate with the Executive Board of Samac municipality concerning the securing of material supplies, so that the returnees could survive, in order to organise the proper functioning of the health system, and those people who were returning, to organise for a doctor to visit the Odzak area, to organise the transport of the population, to organise for transport and set up a bus line, if possible. The public works and the public utilities were to be linked with the communal works in Samac. The Pik factory in Samac was to be linked up with the farms in Odzak or in Novi Grad, and coordinators were to be appointed for that. And through our companies in Samac, they would keep working. But again, only as approved and as ordered by the military administration. You couldn't do anything without their approval and their consent. All those who were in charge of organising this whole thing had to go to the military administration or, rather, to the command, see the commander, talk to him, and obtain approval or permission as to what they could do and what they couldn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, please tell me: As the chief activity, was the return of refugees. This return of refugees, did this apply to all refugees, regardless of their ethnic background, or were any distinctions made?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No distinctions were being made. Everyone was to be received, all those who wished to return. But again, approval had to be obtained, and there was a certain procedure that had to be followed, regardless of whether a person was a Serb, a Croat, or a Muslim. The whole thing had to go through their security organs, and only then could they obtain permission to return to their homes, which means there was no ban, no prohibition against anyone. Whoever wished to return could do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During your work with the council, or the military administration, do you know of any cases where non-Serbs returned to the Odzak area, the area of Odzak municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I know a man who worked with the Red Cross. He was a Croat. And there were a couple of other names too that I can't remember now, but they came and were received. They came there, and no one caused them any trouble. He was even actively involved. This means that all those who wished to, could do so. There were a couple of those who were of a different ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to tender into evidence this document, Your Honour, if there are no objections from the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D185/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Ms. Registrar, I'm /1 in internal -- and Mr. Lukic is /3, and we have /4, Mr. Lazarevic. Of course, "P" is for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you could please give me a moment to find the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Belgrade] [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness can go ahead. We can get the number later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Appropriate time for the break, because I have another document to discuss with this witness, so maybe we shall not have enough time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take our break now and continue our proceedings at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the number of the exhibit first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The number of the last exhibit tendered is D167/1 and ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, let us discuss another document now, that is, the rules for entering the zone of Tactical Group 1 or the military administration zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have three copies for the Trial Chamber and two for registrar and court officer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the booth have one document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Regulations on entering TG 1 zone by various publicly or privately owned firms, et cetera, issued by the commander Colonel Ratomir Simic on April 8th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the booth are asking for a copy, if anything is going to be read, especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. Just to make comments in general, so I don't have intention to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Internal number, for the benefit of our friends from the Prosecution, is ODZ 2. In B/C/S language it's version of one page, and translation is two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, I see -- do you have this document, Regulations of entering the zone of TG 1?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us: How did that work in practice? Because that was an order issued by the commander of the military administration. Tell me: How did it work in practice? I'm particularly interested in the movement of individuals and material and equipment into the military administration zone and outside of the zone. How did it look like in practice?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was like this: Within the civilian domain, we had a secretary or a technical professional who kept record of what the civilian requirements were so that within the area of responsibility, or rather, Odzak municipality, that they can be -- go in or out of the zone. This was done by Mrs. Jelena Zaric. A person was supposed to go to her, give their personal details, and from this document you see that she had to fill out certain forms, then take them to the commander to be approved or to the organ that was in charge of these affairs, and that was in fact Captain Todorovic, the assistant, and it was up to him to approve the request or not approve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, let us summarise. So the person in charge was Captain Todorovic, assistant commander for civilian affairs. Who was his superior, according to hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander, Colonel at the time, it was Ratomir Simic, and before him, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation didn't get all the names.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to their hierarchy --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Popovic. Can you please repeat, starting from Colonel Novica Simic onwards, but slowly, so that we can enter that into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first commander was Major or Lieutenant Colonel Novica Simic. After he left, Lieutenant Colonel Miroslav Bandzur took the office. After that came Colonel Pero Spasojevic, and his successor was Colonel Ratomir Simic. And then later, Milivoje Simic was appointed this duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Popovic, tell me: In case it was necessary for certain works to be done in the area of the military administration, who was it to coordinate the workers and their coming into the area, and who was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, I said that everybody was interconnected in the area of Odzak municipality with certain companies in Samac, in Modrica, Brod. Brod was not very much involved. And the managers or, rather, the coordinators, would come and present their requests concerning, for instance, if it had to do with electricity, then they would come to Krstanovic, Perica, and they would obtain approval to bring some material into or take it out of the area. And at every entry point there were checkpoints manned by military police who inspected the documents, and if a person didn't have an approval from the military administration commander, such person was not allowed either to go out or in. So it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, can you tell us when the Crisis Staff of Samac municipality ceased to operate and when another body started to function, and what was the name of that body?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Please, we are going back to the year of 1992. First there was a Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality, and which body succeeded it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did it start to function?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was sometime in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe you are wrong. When did the Serbian municipality of Samac, when did the Assembly hold its session, the first session?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first session was held in 1992, in late March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Wait, Mr. Popovic. Just slow down, please. First there was a Crisis Staff, and it lasted -- operated until a certain point in time. Then came the War Presidency, then the Municipal Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Samac was held. Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I confused these things a little bit. That was, I think, in December or November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please wait, wait. You're a little bit confused. Mr. Popovic, you -- in July 1992, you went to work on the council, as instructed by the military administration. Which body was established at the time in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know anything about establishing the War Presidency of Samac municipality in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was transformed into a War Presidency composed of three men --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who were those three men on the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, those were Blagoje Simic, Simeon, and myself. The other worked on the Executive Board of the municipality, headed by Milan Simic and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. We have cleared that. Did the War Presidency of Samac municipality, in the period between July 1992 onwards, during several months, was in any way related to the operation of the military administration council?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no relation whatsoever. As an illustration, for example, if I was a member of the War Presidency, I had no reason to go to Samac municipality, to the Executive Board, and try discuss things with people who called themselves ministers, to persuade them that I needed things for the civilians and refugees living there, in terms that I needed food, fuel, seed, et cetera. If I were a superior to that person, why should I go and ask him to do me a favour? I could only -- I could simply give them an order. Because as far as I understood the situation, the War Presidency's role was simply to verify certain formulations presented to us by the Executive Board relating to what they had done in the previous period. And gentlemen, pending the beginning of the Assembly coming into operation, they were just supposed to do that, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did the War Presidency bear any influence on the work obligations from July 1992 onwards that was carried out in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not have any influence. I have to go back again to what was originally agreed, and that is that everyone was supposed to be linked with enterprises in Odzak municipality. So any request would be forwarded to the executive committee or, rather, to the ministry Department of Defence. Based on that, every enterprise, for instance, waterworks, knew what they had to do. So people in Samac involved in this would either send those who were supposed to do the work and issue decisions for their work obligation, and if it was possible, they were paid salaries for the work that they did. This is -- the same was applied for electric power, utility enterprises, and other factors involved. So it was not addressed by the War Presidency, because who was there on the War Presidency? If Savo was in Odzak, Blagoje was alone; Simeon was engaged in information affairs. So there was no need whatsoever, nor was it determined by decisions that this should go through the channel of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If there is no objections from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see none. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document, it's D168/1 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please. Another document that I would like to discuss with this witness is the internal number ODZ 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, it was you who submitted this document to us. On the left-hand corner there is an illegible part, but it refers to an order issued by General Talic, appointing the head of the military administration and other organs. As much as you can recall, can you tell us when this order was issued? Because I see your name under A, under B there was Pavic, Miso Pavic. So do you remember when this order was issued because we can't read it in the left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that that was sent by fax, so that's not very discernible, I think that was in late May or early June 1993, and that this order arrived, as far as I can tell -- there was some ambiguities whether, in the law or the rules governing the military administration, whether it was up to the head or to the chief of court to introduce military administration. And therefore, a new order was issued appointing Colonel Milivoje Simic, who was singled out from the command staff, and he had a special occasion where he had a secretary of his own --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, we had problems with the reception. Just can you please comment on this? Because we see that in this military administration organ, you were appointed officer for economic affairs, whereas the other members covered other areas. Can you tell us: How did it work in practice? What were your particular overall duties?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written here that I was in charge of economic affairs, but when this man was appointed the head of the military administration, he was dislocated from the TG command and he had his own officers. And he invited the people listed here to a meeting, where he said: Gentlemen, based upon the order, I am the head of the military administration, and you are going to do and perform whatever I order you to do. And I think that this kind of order, or the actions taken by Mr. Milivoje Simic were exclusive, and he was the one who maintained all contacts with the command, with the neighbouring municipalities, and he took over these roles and he also went to the Executive Board of Samac and Modrica municipalities and he coordinated work with them.
