We were sort of pushed aside, and I started -- I didn't go to meetings as often as I did, and I didn't have much work to do, because people went solely to him. He talked to them. And whether he consulted someone else or -- I don't know if he did that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, the civilian structures in Samac, more specifically, the president of the Municipal Assembly, Blagoje Simic, at that time - I'm speaking about 1992 - did he have any influence on the work and on the organs of military administration in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way for him to exert any influence there, because the army during that period was such that you had no possibility of talking to them a lot. It was all about them giving orders to you, saying that they needed this or that, so please go and find fuel or anything else that they requested the army. It had to be done, because tasks were in question concerning the defence, and there was no possibility for communication of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Number of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D169/1 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher. Please, could we have your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, now, I have one last document to go through with you, one you forwarded to us. It's a dispatch of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, dated the 2nd of September, 1993. It has to do with the takeover of a certain amount of corn for feeding cattle. My question is the following. It's related to the supply of the fodder for the cattle. How was fodder put aside for the needs of the army, of the Main Staff, on the one hand, and for the republican stocks and supplies, on the other hand, in the zone of the military administration of Odzak? Can you please explain briefly? Who made these requests? How would these requests then be carried out?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the stocks and supplies are concerned, that was on the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence and the republican government exclusively. But as far as the provisions for the army stationed in this area were concerned, a certain company or enterprise based in Samac or Modrica would, for example, have a bakery as part of their company. And there was no more corn, no more wheat. So they would speak to the assistant for civilian affairs, or rather, through the military administration all the way to the assistant for civilian affairs of the corps for the Main Staff to approve some of the supplies that were kept in barns and accumulated throughout the previous period, usually wheat, which was going rot because there was no electricity for circulation over there. So that means the enterprise, the military administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. A specific question: The civilian authorities of Samac municipality, did they have any influence over the way goods, supplies, and materials were distributed in the area of the Odzak military administration?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They couldn't distribute anything, because it was all under the command of the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D170/1 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document under the title of -- it's ODZ 4. It's execution of order, dated September 2nd, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, tell me, please: You remember a member of the War Presidency of Samac, and although you explained there were no such activities, but do you have any personal information that the War Presidency of Samac, in September 1992, requested by a letter the return of a group of the volunteers from Serbia via the Serbian MUP, I mean Lugar, Crni, and other such people? What's your information about that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no part in that, nor was I aware of the existence of any such document requesting the return of volunteers. There were certain assumptions, and there were rumours that the volunteers would be back, because nothing was to be achieved without them. But I think it was merely Stevan Todorovic's propaganda, in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd move to strike. He's speculating at the end of that question: I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. You heard this from Todorovic and there were rumours about town. So as far as I understood, you don't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's a leading question. He just said -- I move to strike because he was just speculating, and then he says, "Fair enough you heard from Todorovic and there were rumours about town." He's testifying for the witness. The witness just said, you know, he thought. The witness was just speculating. Now he's putting -- he's giving the witness an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Don't ask leading questions. The witness was very much in the sphere of things, so he knows what was happening. So simply put questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I follow the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, as you were both a member of the War Presidency, although you spent most of your time in Odzak, still, you were a man who was in possession of certain information. Please tell me accurately: The War Presidency, did it ever send any kind of letter to the MUP of Serbia regarding the return of volunteers, the group including Crni, Lugar, and the rest of them? I'm talking about September 1992.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. What's your information concerning the arrest of that group of volunteers towards the end of 1992? Do you have any knowledge that they were arrested or of their eventual fate, whether any charges were brought against them? Tell us what you know about those events towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group that was active in the area of Samac municipality had links to both the police and the army. They committed certain crimes. They were guilty of mistreatment. Arrests were made by the organs, and those who were under investigation, who were suspected of having committed various crimes -- I never found out myself what exactly had happened over there during their interrogations or during investigations, whether anyone was finally convicted or not. Eventually, those gentlemen left the area of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, tell me, please: Do you have any information? Where were charges brought against them? Before which court?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mostly done by military investigators, and this was, as far as I know, within the framework of Bijeljina and Banja Luka. They were in charge. Banja Luka. That's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information regarding the wounding of Mr. Blagoje Simic? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the summer. It happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992 or 1993. I'm not sure. Give or take a year or two. It's difficult to remember. I think it was back in 1993 or 1992. It was in the summer, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Popovic. You started working for the military administration in 1992, in July. If you bear in mind that moment when you began working there, in relation to that, when was Dr. Blagoje Simic wounded?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you have any knowledge how long Mr. Blagoje Simic took to recover from his wounds? Was he in touch with you? Did he ever go to Odzak in that period?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never went. He was being treated. He was in a rehabilitation period. And I was absent too. I was in Odzak, and the War Presidency ceased to function. And the only man who was there at the time was Mr. Mitar Mitrovic. As far as I know, Stevan Todorovic often came to see Mr. Mitar, and my information was that he had --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object at this time.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- He had written up a document for him to represent the presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question was about Blagoje Simic going to Odzak, and he starts off by talking about Blagoje Simic apparently going to Samac, which is not the question before him, and now he's off on a tangent on Stevan Todorovic. He's not answering the questions. I just move to strike whatever he said and let them start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, let us please try to clarify a number of issues. Firstly, you were in Odzak; Mr. Blagoje Simic had been wounded. My question is: Did Blagoje Simic come to see you in Odzak during that period?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After his wounding, in that period, he never came. And he wasn't able to. In the area of Odzak municipality, Blagoje could only have been there two or three times, to the best of my knowledge. That's when he came to me and spoke to me. Whether he was there without me knowing that he was actually there, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, when was that when you met him there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1992, when we were supposed to go and see Mr. Novica Simic. That was in late August or perhaps in August. That's when he came to Odzak. And we spoke to Mr. Novica Simic, and then we were off to Osjecani. Throughout 1992, he did come another time. It was in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Mr. Popovic, there's a story developing here in the course of certain testimonies by Prosecution witnesses. Was there any kind of pool next to the singer Meho Puzic's house in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the pool is still there, and it was there. I'm not sure why the reference to the pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was this pool being used while you were in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't be used, because in that period of time there was no electricity. Generators were being used to pump water, sporadically. Sometimes generators were used to provide water for the command building and its close surroundings, but not to top up a pool for someone to take a swim. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Mr. Blagoje Simic ever having been there, near that pool in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What do you know about Mr. Blagoje Simic being wounded and then after that who was the head of the War Presidency in Samac, in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I started talking about, and that's why there was a misunderstanding. After Blagoje had been wounded, the three of us were practically -- Mitar as a lawyer was there in those rooms, and I was informed later that Mr. Todorovic had abused the War Presidency, misused the War Presidency, and that a document was signed for him that he could speak on behalf of the War Presidency and that he went somewhere to the government or wherever, I don't know where he could go and where he could introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases of robberies in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, there were a number of robberies. But the situation we were in as civilians, or as civilian authorities, the military security were in charge of everything. It was all down to them. They had their own organs, and Odzak municipality was surrounded by checkpoints manned by military police officers. And inside, we had a department of the Samac police station, headed by Mirko Pavic. Their role, their task, was to protect property, property that was in the area. However, there was, and certainly there are cases where people with a carton of cigarettes, or after being bribed, could take whatever they liked, through the checkpoints at night, those people there. Certainly they could. I was in no position to control that. But yes, everything was hermetically cut off by the military administration, that is, the command of the Tactical Group number 1, the checkpoints of the military police, and you couldn't pass through, you couldn't go in or out without them stopping you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, can you please tell us: How would you describe that on the basis of your personal information? Was that organised robbery, with orders being given and plans being drafted, or were those random, individual cases which occur in peacetime, let alone in war? How would you describe that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've seen the instructions a while ago. The military administration had the authority to move goods from one area to another. Now, whether the military administration or the command did anything without the organs of civilian authority knowing about it, they could use lorries to take stuff away. They didn't have to report to me, but I do have information or, more specifically, I know that some of the equipment had been moved to the area of responsibility of the Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During those operations where equipment was being moved, did Blagoje Simic play any role in that, or any civilian bodies from Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic, as the president of the presidency, could not have anything to do with it. If something was needed for the needs of the Executive Board of Samac municipality, the Executive Board would go through the military administration or an enterprise from Samac municipality through the military administration. Whether something was needed for the territory of Odzak municipality, iron, cement, building materials, corn, wheat, that part which could have been in function of Samac municipality. So that the needs of the population could be met, those who were returning to the area of Odzak, and refugees who were located in Samac municipality. That means, again, you need to have papers to cover what you needed and who would approve or not approve the commander of the military administration. If he approved, you could take things out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, how many Serbian refugees were returned to the territory of Odzak municipality? Can you give us some numbers?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between five and six thousand Serbs were returned. But in early 1993, based on the approval of the military administration and some higher organs, refugees from around Zavidovici and Maglaj and other municipalities started pouring in into Odzak, and they were given accommodation in the town and the surrounding villages. So very soon, until mid-1993, there were some 10 or 11.000 civilians in the territory of Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After the Dayton Accord, do you know how many Serbs, roughly speaking, remained in the territory of Odzak municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I worked for another company, but as far as I know, all the Serbs have left the municipality, although they thought they could stay. But somebody ordered -- gave an order, the Dayton Accords were signed, and nearly 100 per cent of the Serbs left the municipality of Odzak. Maybe a dozen persons were left. I'm not sure, because I was not involved very much in those events at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know, in late 1992, was there any information signed by the 2nd Posavina Brigade command relating to the situation in Samac municipality? Do you know anything about this document and the reasons for drawing up that document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know, and I know who wrote this information. That was Mr. Simo Zaric, who prepared that information. I don't know on whose orders that was done, but that was subject of consideration at the level of Posavina Brigade command, and the desire was to create an atmosphere through such information that it was somebody else among the civilian authorities doing robberies, that they were not satisfied, and they were not performing along the lines of the army that was covering a 2-kilometre-long front. And I believe that this is where certain disagreement occurred among a number of personnel who imposed themselves in early 1992 -- in early 1991 and 1992, but due to the lack of competence, they failed to perform some other duties, and that is what I believed how it was. And I am positive that they were infiltrated -- or rather, assigned to this brigade, saying that this one is going to be in charge of morale, the other was going to be in charge of technical matters, and you cannot be a battalion commander any longer because the army didn't want to have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Popovic: According to what you know, what was the reason and what was the background of this information being drawn up?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The background was, in fact, to launch a sort of coup against the legal organs, and that was the civilian authorities and War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the gentlemen who were then on the Tactical Group command and who wrote this information. So it is easy to see who those people were, and if you allow me, one of the signatories asked me very often: How come that I was on the War Presidency? Who was I elected by? And that was Mr. Tubakovic and some others whose names I wouldn't like to mention. So due to that, they wanted to create such a climate within the units and to carry out a sort of coup and to bring some other people in, in order to take over these duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Most of his testimony in the last few minutes doesn't even make any sense. However, his indication of what the intent was -- persons who filed the document is not proper. They can -- Mr. -- there's testimony indicating Mr. Zaric will testify. We've had Marko Tubakovic who was one of the signatories testifying in Belgrade. Those are the people who can indicate what the intent was on drafting that document and publishing that document, not this gentleman who is technically being accused of certain crimes or inadequacies in that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe this is a matter for cross-examination. This is a personal knowledge of this particular witness of the reasons and bases for this document, nothing more. So I don't see any particular problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pantelic. The problem is that he is talking about the intentions of the people who wrote that document, and that's what the Prosecution is objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that with -- it's hearsay. I mean, that's a standard here. But I will clarify gladly with the witness, then. It might be hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure what he wants to do. I'll have to wait and see and determine the relevance then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, according to your personal knowledge, tell me: Were there any attempts at setting -- at convening a meeting of the Municipal Assembly in late 1992 and 1993; and if there were, who initiated that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, exactly, precisely, those people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which people?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signatories of this document, of this information, requesting the municipal assembly to be convened, where many issues could be clarified. Whether that was true what was contained in this information or not, but nevertheless, the assembly was convened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What conclusions were made at the assembly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions were that everything remained much the same as it were, because many things were not contained in the information, for instance, that the War Presidency was not the initiator of the events mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the Municipal Assembly accept this information or reject it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They rejected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did any of the signatories or any other military personnel want to have a place in civilian authorities? But briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to give you specific answers, but it turned out that I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once again, I'd object, and he said the same thing. He's talking about the intention of military authorities to have a place, whatever that means, in civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can say if he heard anything like that. And also, Mr. Pantelic, in order for the record to make sense, I wanted to find out the exhibit number of this document in which this information was contained, because it's been discussed at length. It's an exhibit, isn't it, I think. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I could help. P127, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: P127, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Popovic, very briefly, tell me: What do you personally know about the motives and intents of the signatories of this document? What was their specific desire?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their wish was to change the civilian authorities in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since you cooperated with Dr. Blagoje Simic, tell me: Was Dr. Blagoje Simic in any manner involved in military operations on the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he could not have been involved in these operations, because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object at this point. He's saying as far as he knows; he's speculating at this point. There's no indication he was with Dr. Simic. He indicated he was home sleeping in Crkvina. He wasn't even in Bosanski Samac. And now he starts off: "As far as I know," which means he's speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, did Blagoje Simic, while you worked together on the Crisis Staff and other organs, tell you that he had played a role in bringing in the volunteers from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now Mr. Pantelic is testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is a leading question, Mr. Pantelic. Maybe you are through with this witness. That's why you're having a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just a couple of questions with regard to the -- I'll finish with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, Mr. Popovic: As a member of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, did you, or did these bodies, take any discriminatory decisions against non-Serbs in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We have never adopted such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did the Crisis Staff of Samac municipality pass a decision to isolate Croats or to place them on vital facilities in the town?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Blagoje Simic ever display discriminatory attitude towards non-Serbs in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. If I can give you an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days, Mr. Blagoje Simic told me, when we were in Uniglas, that I should go and fetch Esap Zaimbegovic, because he was a former manager of that company, and I did go and bring Mr. Zaimbegovic, and he started working in his company and started organising the work. Later, Mr. Todorovic made up the document and he detained -- imprisoned that man and mistreated him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I said we didn't need the extra details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I just got it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The answer was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Popovic: Did Mr. Blagoje Simic, in any way whatsoever, take part in military operations in the area of Samac municipality, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once again, it's leading. There's no basis of knowledge. He's not indicating any time period. It's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The time frame I established -- obviously, it's mid-April 1992 until the end of 1993. That was the line of questioning. But I will clarify that gladly with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Popovic, tell me: Since you were in touch with Blagoje Simic, you spent quite some time with him, you worked together on this organ, so you have certain personal knowledge, tell me everything that you know about that. Did Mr. Blagoje Simic make any connections with military structures or volunteers from Serbia? What is your personal knowledge about that? Because you were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object. Once again, this witness has testified he was in Crkvina -- I'm sorry. Not Crkvina. Odzak, from July of 1992 to March of 1993. He's saying: Since you were there, tell us about this. He wasn't with Blagoje Simic. How can he answer whether or not he made any contact? They weren't together. How can he answer whether or not they had any connections?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be a period before July, before he went to Odzak. I think it's up to you, Mr. Pantelic, to specify which period you are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, I'm referring to the period of mid-April 1992 until July, when you joined the military administration in Odzak. I'm also speaking about your personal knowledge about the period until the end of 1993, because occasionally you met Mr. Blagoje Simic. So I'm covering this precise period.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely saying Blagoje did not have any possibility to give orders or to cooperate or to command military forces because they didn't want that, they didn't request that. The only communication line with them was if they needed something, those needs were to be need [sic]. From late July until the end of 1993, in addition to what I mentioned, that this gentleman came two or three times, I also went to Samac, at least two or three times a week, to the municipality of Samac, and I also dropped by to the premises where Blagoje was. Therefore, I had contacts with Mr. Blagoje Simic relating to the operation of the War Presidency. So I was in a position to know if something happened or did not happen. How could anyone do something on my behalf or on behalf of the War Presidency without my knowing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, did Mr. Blagoje Simic ever issue an order to arrest non-Serbs from Samac and to be subjected to maltreatment and other --

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't give such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: While you were a member of the Crisis Staff between April and between the time it ceased to operate, how would you describe it? Was that a single-party concept? Were you all members of the same political party or was it established in a different shape politically, and how you worked together?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a single-party establishment. I was not a member of either the SDS or any other political party. And yesterday I said that I left --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you be precise, please, and just speak about the Crisis Staff. Time is precious.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a single-party establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which party were on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of any political party, and Mr. Blagoje Simic was a liberal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We had some difficulties, technical difficulties, and we'll go back to the beginning. According to what you know, can you give us full names? Because there were two Simic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Blagoje Simic was member of the SDS. Savo Popovic was not a member of any party. Simic was member of the liberal league. He was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are referring to Simeon Simic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Simeon Simic, and Bozo Ninkovic were liberals. Mr. Tadic, as far as I know, was not a member of any party. Therefore, for instance, this Fadil Topcagic also, as far as I know, was not a member of any political party. Therefore, those were the people, and also Mr. Mirko Jovanovic, who was a member of the SDS, and Mitar, as a technical secretary, was a member of the SDS. So that was everything concerning these political party affiliations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do you personally know about whether an instruction arrived from some higher SDS organs at the level of the Republika Srpska about the creation of the Crisis Staff in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I -- and you'll ask me again as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just tell me what you know.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about anything about this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff draft any plan with the 17th Tactical Group and Colonel Nikolic? Do you know anything about such plan?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody made any plans with the Crisis Staff, because practically, by entering the town and the fighting, we started to gather together and to form this body called Crisis Staff. Therefore, neither I nor other people were able to participate in drawing up any plans. That was exclusively a military matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was a military matter?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the attack on Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm Branko Lukic. I'm defending Mr. Miroslav Tadic. I have merely two questions for you. One is a question proper and another is just a clarification following from your answers to my colleague Mr. Pantelic. We found out from your testimony today that Mr. Milos Bogdanovic was a blood relation of yours, a brother-in-law. I found out today.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurdjevic, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is related to Milos Bogdanovic, because you said he had provided a lot of your information, that you socialised with him. Mr. Milos Bogdanovic, did he ever tell you that there had been a list where his arrest was being planned, his arrest and other persons to be arrested, by Stevan Todorovic, specifically?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic said - and I had occasion to hear this from Debeli also, because he didn't know my last name - that Mr. Bogdanovic, Simo Zaric, Fadil Topcagic, Savo Popovic, Milos Bogdanovic, there was a possibility for them, as they were among the leftists, the communists, there was a possibility, a likelihood, for them to be killed. And I asked Debeli: Do you know my name? And he said: I know your name is Savo. And I said: I'm Savo Popovic. And he blushed, and he went pale, and he said: Forget all I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about liquidations, killings. I said: Do you know, were you familiar with the fact or did he tell you about a list of names written up by Stevan Todorovic, including Miroslav Tadic, that he too was to be arrested? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He told me. Milos told me. And this is just to corroborate. I just want to describe how exactly it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Just an additional clarification. During your testimony, you referred to -- after your arrival in Odzak several days later, you said that Miroslav Tadic came, in connection with civilian protection affairs. And after that, you told us about the council and you told us about who the members of the council were. I just want that clarification. Miroslav Tadic, did he have anything to do with that council, or was he only there in connection with civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to Odzak in relation to civilian protection affairs. He was there to arrange and help with the arrangements surrounding the return of civilians who were returning from camps, wherever they were. And from time to time, he would come with those people. We would welcome them there. They would be received and accommodated. He wasn't based there --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've lost part of the answer again due to technical problems. You said he didn't go there all the time. Can you just repeat the last part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come at the time when people who had been detained in camps would arrive. He came when bus loads of them arrived. He made sure they could go to their homes or that accommodation was provided for them, because some of their houses had been burnt. So that was his task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Popovic. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic. I'm defending Mr. Simo Zaric before this Tribunal. I only have several questions to ask you in relation to what you testified today. One question is related to what Mr. Lukic has already asked you. Another question is related to a session, to a meeting of the Crisis Staff. You already spoke about Simo Zaric, that he was supposed to be in charge of what you called national security. Let me ask you the following: There was a certain meeting of the Crisis Staff after that, attended also by Stevan Todorovic. Mr. Zaric's appointment was debated at that meeting. First of all, let me ask you: Were you there? Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did Stevan Todorovic say anything in connection with Simo Zaric being a traitor of the Serbian people, that he had been arresting Serbs and that it would have been completely inadequate to name him as chief of national security? Did you attend anything like this?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic knew full well that Mr. Zaric had been nominated for national security, and there was no way for him to come to terms with that. He just couldn't come to terms with that. National security or chief of police, that these posts would be filled by Simo Zaric. He was only looking for a way all the time to prevent Mr. Zaric from doing the job, and he employed all kinds of methods. He was exerting pressure for Mr. Zaric to be removed from that position, from that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me now just ask you something with respect to the information that Mr. Pantelic had asked you about. This is Exhibit Number 527 [as interpreted]. I will not go into details of that particular paper, but if you could please just remember: There is also mention of Colonel Djurdjevic's, your relative's, removal or dismissal in that information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In that paper, in that information, the issue of volunteers or special troops, depending on the term being used, their crimes in Crkvina, the murders, that's also something that's referred to or mentioned in the information; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We could say that the information, the paper, condemns the crimes?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. But the crimes are being attributed to the Crisis Staff, to the civilian sector, that is, to the Executive Board, that many things, that means, went through those channels or those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After that, the information also speaks about robberies, which you have also referred to as a concomitant of the war in Bosanski Samac, a side effect, and this is also condemned, not merely the fact that the robberies were committed by civilians, but rather also the army is being condemned, because even among its ranks there were robberies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, in this paper, frequent changes, frequent removals of commanders in the army are also condemned, by saying that it has very detrimental effect on the soldiers' morale.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We could go on to say that all these were negative or detrimental phenomena that were only to be condemned, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could certainly say that. Some people who had arrived from somewhere else and drawn up that paper and stated all that. But those people who drew up the paper were people who were there from the beginning, and now you could ask which of them took any measures, the signatories and the participants, while they were in their respective positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Apologies. Due to technical problems, I think we didn't get -- or I think we actually did receive your specific reply. I certainly agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lazarevic. Just for the clarity of the record, I think the exhibit you're talking about should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, because on page 67, line 2, it says Exhibit 527.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. It's P127, just for clarity of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another question related to this information paper. After this information paper was in some way made public, a meeting was held at the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Did you attend that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I did, but maybe that was in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's where the brigade command was based, in Pelagicevo. Can you please tell me now: How did the meeting go? How did it develop? What happened during that meeting? What subjects were discussed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only about the information paper and about the data contained therein, whether it was true or not, specifically in relation to certain documents and who did it and why something was done, and which measures could be taken and who would have had to take these measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me briefly about the atmosphere at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Popovic. My name is Phillip Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm going to be asking you some questions.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you testified yesterday that in -- that you had been a member of the League of Communists for approximately 25 years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you testified that approximately in 1988, 1989, you had quit or left the League of Communists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that during that period you had been involved -- you had been politically active with the League of Communists, not just a common or run-of-the-mill member; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My convictions have remained the same, but I no longer wanted to work in the League of Communists. I was a member of the municipal committee and I stopped going to its sessions. But I was still associated with my local organisation, local branch of the League of Communists in Crkvina, and I was in charge of a number of duties. I was a member of the council of the local commune. I was president of the local football club. So I was interested in how life was going on in the local commune. There was no other party there, to all intents and purposes. That was the only organised form of political activity there. But the meetings were not frequent. There would be several meetings in a year, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you stayed active, at least politically, locally, in Crkvina, for a while, after you left the League of Communists; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then, in 1993, you joined the SDS party; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1993, or 1994. I'm not sure. I'm not sure about the time period, but I know that I did join, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at that time, there were other parties that you had the option of joining, but you joined the SDS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the socialist party, the SDP, was still in existence, but I had no reason to associate myself or to work with people who then became the leaders of the SDP. So my choice, in view of certain convictions and views that were included or embodied, rather, in the platform of the SDS, and I believe that leftists could feel at home in that party, that's why I chose to join the SDS. Now that you're asking me about this, a number of former members or associates started working with the SDS, and then when they saw that they couldn't, they went back to the SDP or to another political party. However, I stayed, and I can't say that I am an active member of the SDS. I'm simply more present there. I didn't hold any office within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you joined the SDS, apparently you agreed with their policies, you were comfortable with them. Did you agree with their policies?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't necessarily mean -- if I joined the SDS, that I had to accept everything. You know, there was a difference of opinions there. So I was in a position to express my agreement or disagreement. I didn't necessarily accept everything that was being said within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I agree that you probably didn't accept everything, but did you overall agree with their policies?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted the platform, the party programme, the original one. But certain documents were then changed, and those who did it, those who took part in that, didn't consult me or ask me for my acceptance. I could either choose to agree or to disagree as a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know who their leaders are, who their national leaders are. Did you respect and agree with their leaders?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The national leaders in 1992 and 1993, the national leader was Mr. Karadzic for the SDS, Alija Izetbegovic, and Boban. All three of them led their own parties, led their own peoples, practically. And at that moment, until it was clear who was what kind of person and where they were leading us, it was very difficult for a politician to assess the true worth of a politician, whether he was good or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about the other leaders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the SDS. Did you agree or respect the SDS leaders when you joined in 1993 and 1994? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, I respected them, but I did have a number of disagreements with the way they worked and with their policies within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And you have remained in that party, after joining in 1993, 1994, even though its three main leaders have been charged with war crimes and genocide; isn't that true? You've remained in that party, those leaders who you indicated you respected?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did remain. It doesn't mean that if the leaders were that the whole people for that and those who were members of the SDS would come into a situation -- that I would leave the SDS because of that. Progressive people, you have progressive people in every political party. I had and I saw a number of people who remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've remained in the party even though one of its leaders, Biljana Plavsic, has recently admitted to the persecution of the non-Serb population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including murders, unlawful detentions, forced expulsions, cruel and inhumane treatment. You've remained in that party even after she has admitted that the SDS formulated a campaign of persecution against the non-Serb population. You've still remained in that party.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, well, this is a leading question, I believe, in connection with Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. What she admitted to, I saw this on TV and I read this in the papers, her statements and what happened with her. I cannot speak about Biljana Plavsic, simply because down the chain of command -- or up the chain of command, I had absolutely no contact whatsoever with her. I was not any part of the SDS bodies, so I can't judge this. If she admitted to whatever she has admitted to, that was her own personal thing, and I'm in no position to judge what she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, she has admitted that she committed these crimes with the other SDS leaders and the Bosnian Serb leaders, and even though she has admitted that they all have orchestrated a campaign of persecution against the non-Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have remained in that same SDS party; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's her own individual. We can't speak collectively about a people or a party, that we're all genocidal, if Mrs. Plavsic was or if a circle of people was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, she was the president of the party while you were a member.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President, yes, the president of that party, but then she changed and she set up a new party altogether, and that's where she was president too. Therefore, she was president of the entity. These political issues, I wouldn't like to be involved, I wouldn't like to start guessing whether she was or not. I had no contact with Biljana. I can't judge her in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on, then. You've remained in that party even after the massacre of over 7.000 Muslims in Srebrenica. You've still remained in that party; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I really don't know where my learned friend found that the massacre in Srebrenica is related to the policy of SDS or each particular -- maybe in order not to confuse this witness, my learned friend can be more specific, saying what are the charges. That's one issue. And the other issue: I don't know why we're wasting so much time here about all these issues, because the presumption of innocence is one of the most important fundamental issues in all legal systems, and all these peoples are only charged. There is no conviction. There is no judgement. So I don't know why we are going through all these issues by this way. So the bottom line is that my learned friend should be more specific when he's putting a question to this witness. And I believe that there is not any single word in all indictments within the Office of the Prosecutor where the SDS, as the institution, is charged. And it is furthermore underlined in the report of Secretary-General of the UN in this Court is not to established to establish the responsibility of institutions but only individual criminal responsibility. So I really don't know why he's building up, you know -- or maybe he has intention to make some bans on political life, ban on the SDS in Bosnia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue of SDS goes to this witness's credibility. In the Plavsic factual basis, which is an exhibit, I believe Exhibit 164 of this Court, it says in paragraph 16: "The main staff of the VRS was responsible to the presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And it indicates who that was composed by. "In addition to its authority over the VRS, the collective presidency -- expanded collective presidencies with supreme authority or the Bosnian police Territorial Defence and civilian authorities. The members of the SDS leadership and the expanded collective presidency made contributions to the objective of ethnic separation by force. Karadzic and Krajisnik, the two pre-eminent and controlling figures in the SDS and the Bosnian government exercised primary power and control over the Bosnian Serb structures." Also, in the Krstic judgement, they indicate, they go right up the line. They indicate who the military was, who the military leader was, and again --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the counsel slow down, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are too fast, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. In view of the military, the military leadership, and on top of them is the collective presidency, the Serb SDS mixture presidency. They're one and the same. Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. You are through?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the Prosecution is entitled to put these questions, for purposes of testing the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You have joined the party of the SDS and remained a member, even after the 12th of May of 1992, when the presidents of the National Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, also an SDS leader, issued a decision of the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Objective number 1 is establish state borders --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities. You have remained in that party even after the policy of your party has been to separate ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. This witness said that he joined the party in 1993 or 1994, so I don't know what is the relation with this date of 12th of May, 1992. It's out of the scope of membership of this witness. It's not related. It's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's not irrelevant because, Your Honour, that's the policy, and Biljana Plavsic has pled guilty to being part of that policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, and it came before the witness decided to join, so he was joining with full knowledge of all these things that were going on within the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour, it would be better for this witness -- or to ask whether he was informed about the strategies to lay a foundation, and then he can clarify that. Because otherwise it's too vague. It's too abstract, to my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pantelic. There's no basis for your objection. The witness knows what he was doing. He's an adult. He decided to join a party, and he can answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: You've joined the party, the SDS party, even after one of its major leaders, Momcilo Krajisnik, as president of the National Assembly, issued a decision of the strategic objectives of the Serbian people, where he stated that the strategic objectives or priorities of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina are to establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It was not the order of Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. He was a speaker of the national parliament. And we have in this particular case, in this particular hearings, proof. It's a Prosecution Exhibit. It was published in the Official Gazette. It was the decision of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, where at that time Mr. Krajisnik only was a speaker. So I think it's not fair what my learned friend just did, to input and to confuse this witness with this assumption that Mr. Krajisnik issued order. It was not true. It's not true, and he can clarify in his own exhibits that it is not the case, simply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's well clarified in Exhibit P5, which has been an exhibit in this case since really the beginning of this case, in September of 2001, where Momcilo Krajisnik has signed that decision as president.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of the National Assembly, as a speaker, he's not issued that order. That is the basis of my objection. And it is not a party document. We have to be clear with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He was the president of the Main Board of the SDS from the 12th of July, 1991, onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will make a quote, Your Honour. Page 77, line 5. Sir, my question was: You joined the party, the SDS party, even after one of its major leaders Momcilo as the president issued a decision, issued a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was not a subject to issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Signed the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pantelic. I hope Mr. Weiner will look into that and explain it after our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In what capacity the decision was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll resume our proceedings at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let us continue again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think you begin with explaining the status of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's a decision -- it's -- it's Exhibit P5. It's a decision on the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those were the six strategic objectives. It's signed by Momcilo Krajisnik, who is president of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, just for the clarity of the transcript, I believe it is not in dispute that this order was adopted by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. Am I right, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, and you joined the party, isn't it true, after SDS leader and president of the National Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, signed an order of the National Assembly of the Serbian people, and this was an order or a decision on strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the first objective was "to establish state borders or priorities in the Serbian people" -- I'm sorry - of the Serbian people -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I misread that. "To establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just to object, Your Honour. It's of significant importance whether it is order or decision. So my learned friend, in his question, tried to mix these two -- these two terms, and I believe that he should be more specific. And maybe to put this document, this Exhibit P5 in front of witness and then he can finally familiarise himself, and then we shall know what is that, order or decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Would you please sit down. The Prosecution will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "Decision on the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And number 1 "strategic objective is to establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities," and it was signed by Momcilo Krajisnik, who was the president of the National Assembly and who, as you also know, was a national SDS leader. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order or, better to say, the decision, I have never heard of it, because I joined the SDS in late 1993. Nobody informed me of that. And I think that the work was sort of frozen, so I didn't know any details. So people who joined the SDS just had paper, but there were no meetings. By the end of 1993, nobody ever showed me or presented this document to me on the presidency. If it did exist, it had -- it was with somebody on the -- with the Executive Board or it was published in the Official Gazette. However, I did not have an opportunity to read this Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you agree with that policy, to establish state borders separating the Serb people from the other two ethnic communities? Did you agree with that policy?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not have an opportunity to read this decision, or whether that policy pursued the idea of having only Serbian population in one area, I wouldn't accept this kind of decision. Why would we have only Serbs living in a specific territory? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was the strategic objective. And are you further aware, sir, that Radovan Karadzic stated, at the Bosnian Serb assembly on the 25th of February, 1992, once the party has adopted a policy, anything else is treason. Anything outside the adopted policy is treason. Were you aware that Radovan Karadzic, Serb leader and SDS leader, issued that order, or actually issued that statement? If you disagree with those policies, it's treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Maybe, in order to clarify this issue -- Is it a statement? Is it a newspaper article? Is it -- if something of this what my learned friend just stated is a part of certain statement, we should know that, because out of context we cannot discuss that. And it's absolutely confusing to our witness. So maybe we could be more specific with that: Where and when and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think there is anything confusing the witness here. The questions is quite clear. Stop disrupting the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe -- I don't know, maybe for you it's clear, but for me it's unclear. Because he said 25th of February, 1992. He made a precise date. My learned friend made a precise date. But what do we know? We don't know whether it's a statement in newspaper, in news conference, on television, et cetera. So that's why. It's page 81, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner did say that this was on line 8 that Mr. Karadzic stated this at the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 25th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now I'm asking: Is it a transcript of what he said exactly? Because everyone can interpret what -- this is serious issues, Your Honour. It's criminal proceedings. We have to be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, will you please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Your objection doesn't make sense. Just sit down. And stop interrupting the proceedings unnecessarily. Mr. Weiner, will you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, as I told you previously, Radovan Karadzic stated or said in a speech at the Bosnian Serb Assembly of the 25th of February, 1992: "Once the party has adopted a policy, anything else is treason. Anything outside the adopted policy is treason." Are you aware of that statement or policy by Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I -- at that period, I wasn't a member of the SDS and this statement of his, if it did take place, was not in any way binding for me, as it was binding perhaps for their members, it didn't apply to me. So it couldn't affect me in any way. My convictions were of an entirely different nature of what he perhaps stated or demanded. As I said yesterday and I said today, I am a leftist by conviction, and therefore that cannot be connected with me in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to make sure that I understand your answer. Are you saying that if you had been a member of the SDS, that statement or policy of Radovan Karadzic would have been binding on you? Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period that you mention, I wasn't a member of the SDS. Therefore, that wasn't binding for me. But it does not mean that if I agree to join the SDS, that I had to follow blindly everything that everyone ordered. So there were some progressive things in that party, but it was up to me personally to decide whether I would agree with such statements made by certain officials or not. In addition, I was not a member of any SDS bodies for me to be able to know everything that they spoke at the sessions of these bodies and what they agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we move on, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified today concerning the creation of the Crisis Staff, and you indicated that it all was -- or basically I'm summarising your testimony: It was all somewhat accidental. You accidentally showed up. While there, Mirko Jovanovic came up with the idea to establish a Crisis Staff. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I came with Mr. Milos Bogdanovic to Pik and that certain discussions took place there, to the effect that a body should be established to coordinate the economic life, the cultural life, all spheres of life, so that we can serve the people. Among other things, they offered me to become one of those people. And I said: If that's what you mean, and if there are no other solutions, and if I can be of any help, I will accept to be at the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you weren't invited to that meeting. You didn't receive any notice or invitation to attend a meeting concerning the establishment of a Crisis Staff. Did that happen, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Other people know that I mainly spent time with Mr. Milos Bogdanovic. We were family friends. I knew that he was not a member of the SDS, and I had information -- he often invited me: Come with me to hear what is going to be discussed at this or that meeting. So among other things, all was done through his work, and that is how I came about or learned about certain things, and that is how it happened that I went together with him to Pik and established these contacts. I did not receive any invitation to come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Milos Bogdanovic receive an invitation to come to a meeting for the establishment of a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he had a different role, as a man, as the head of the department for ministry, and there was no need for him to be invited or not invited. I know that at that time, there were no invitations sent out to anyone. This is the first time that I hear of any invitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, so is it your testimony it was only a group of people sitting around talking, and the idea of a Crisis Staff arose? That's basically what you testified to. There was no plan on that date to establish a Crisis Staff. A group of people all just happened upon the Pik company, wound up in a conversation, and a Crisis Staff was established; is that the gist of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. A group of people got together. I was among them. And we discussed how to organise ourselves. And since others did the same, it was suggested that it be done within a certain body to be called Crisis Staff, and that is why I said that the first four men, the already-mentioned gentlemen, and others later were included in this Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, before we get back to the -- I'm sorry. Sir, before we get back to the Crisis Staff, I just want to make it clear: You had attended some meetings prior to this meeting at the Pik. You attended the meeting in February concerning the establishment of a Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, and you also attended the meeting and election in Obudovac, on March 28th; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you there throughout both of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, because I was interested to hear what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you agree, sir, that you have not been truthful with this Court today concerning the information relating to the Crisis Staff? Your testimony has not been truthful; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which parts you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that at the March meeting, there was discussion concerning the establishment of a Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I was present at the memorial centre when the Samac assembly was established, and I also said that in late March an assembly session was held again in Obudovac, where I also was present, and I started describing how certain organs were elected by the assembly and the Executive Board, but I was interrupted and I didn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we place on the ELMO so the witness could see Exhibit P124, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Turn to page 14, which is a decision, and it's a March 28, 1992, Article 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could he please turn to page 14 in the English, or on the B/C/S it's Article 1 of March -- decision March 28th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I invite your attention to Article 1 of that decision of March 28th, 1992. Can you see it in front of you on the monitor? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It says: "Because of the beginning of war operations against the Serbian people, the Samac Municipal Assembly charges the president of the municipal board of the Serbian Democratic Party in Samac and the president of the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation to form the municipal Crisis Staff immediately. The municipal Crisis Staff shall be composed of representatives of political, military, and other institutions of the Serbian people." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, I see it, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us read Article 2.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was this decision written?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, March 28th, it was decided, the meeting that you attended, sir. Let us move on to Article 2: "The municipal assembly hereby authorises the Crisis Staff to exercise the functions of the highest organ of authority of the Serbian people --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me, sir? We've had some technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll continue on: "To exercise the functions of the highest organs of the authority of the Serbian people within the scope of the rights and duties of the municipality and to pass decisions and other regulations within the jurisdiction of the Municipal Assembly if conditions do not permit it to convene." Do you see that, sir? Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go to the first page, which has a preamble, as we would call it, a summary prior to the decisions being listed, and it's just one sentence I'd like to read. The fourth paragraph, which is just one sentence, and it says -- thank you, Mr. Usher: "The Crisis Staff was formed in the St. Sava hall of the Church of the Holy Mother in Obudovac on the 15th of April, 1992." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the Crisis Staff was established on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And sir, could you look at the cover page of this. This is the Official Gazette, municipality of Samac, year 1, number 1, Friday, 3 June, 1994, Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see the date, 1st of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, let's move on. You talked about the appointment of individuals at that meeting. Could we please move to page 12 in the English, and let me see the B/C/S, please. Sir, you testified about certain people being appointed, certain names coming up, being appointed to various positions. I'd like you to look at Article 1 of the -- from that same meeting that you attended on the 28th of March, 1992. Were you present for the elections of those persons listed there to the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly of Samac? Were you present for those elections?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the audience. I was not actively involved. I know that they were elected, members of the Executive Council of the Serbian municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you'll notice that Mirko Jovanovic was elected president of the Executive Council at that meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if you heard the question because of technical difficulties. You'll notice that Mirko Jovanovic was elected president of the Executive Council at that meeting. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in addition, you'll notice that Milos Bogdanovic was elected secretary of the municipal secretariat of National Defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC [Resumed]
